input:
The steady-state conversion for the neutralisation that is carried out in the continuous stirred-tank reactor comes out at 94.3%. This figure is the ideal-CSTR value corresponding to the stated rate constant and residence time, and it should be understood as carrying with it all of the idealisations that are built into that particular model.

The reaction in question is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.273 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 61 min, and the two quantities enter into the conversion through their product: $k\tau$ = 0.273 x 61 = 16.65. For an ideal CSTR at steady state, the conversion is given by $X = \frac{k\tau}{1 + k\tau}$, where $X$ denotes the conversion and the denominator reflects the dilution of the reacting mixture by the material that is already present in the vessel. Substituting $k\tau$ = 16.65 into this relation gives $X$ = 94.3%. A product $k\tau$ of this magnitude stands well into the flat part of the relation: the conversion is high essentially because the residence time is long in comparison with the rate constant, and a moderate change in either quantity would move the result only slightly.

It is important to note the assumptions on which the estimate rests, namely perfect mixing and constant density. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not in fact been run, which means that the mixing behaviour of the actual vessel remains unverified: the presence of dead zones or of short-circuiting in the vessel would cause part of the feed to pass through in less than the mean residence time, and would bring the actual conversion down below the ideal value. The 94.3% figure is therefore the conversion of the ideal reactor at the stated conditions, and should be presented as such; the actual vessel can only be measured against it once a tracer test, or a direct measurement at the outlet, has supplied the comparison that is needed.
